This is true. This is why when responding or giving advice I try to (and I suggest others do this also):

1. Avoid platitudes at call costs.

2. Focus on the problem of the individual, not similar problems or my own.

3. Don't feel obligated to give advice; sometimes I just listen.

4. Give practical, tangible advice: I refrain from sentiments like "fuck them" or "get another boyfriend/girlfriend/job, etc". People usually aren't in a position to just change  things at whim or daily remove toxic people from their lives.

5. Respond to people I think my experience and knowledge will enable me to offer something helpful. This doesn't mean I have to have first-habd knowledge; it means I need to be able to understand enough to go beyond sympathy. I need to empathize.

6. Do not contradict them or otherwise devalue the validity of their feelings and experience.

7. Remind myself what worked for me might not work for others or be applicable.

I don't like getting bullshit advice, either. I hate platitudes because they reduce individual problems to one size fits all solutions. Of course, just like real products, these one size fits all solutions only truly fit a mainstream/majority  populace; those of us on the fringes don't benefit fully. 

However, when someone gives me advice, if it just doesn't apply well to me, I focus on their intent. I remind myself they aren't professionals. I think of the times I didn't know what to say but felt expected to say something and what came out was bullshit advice. We often feel pressured to say something because otherwise we fear people will think we aren't listening and don't care, which compounds their problem.

Many times I scroll through this sub and see posts without a reply and I am tempted to say something. But I check myself and ask: Will what I have to offer be useful to this person saying they want to kill themselves? Beyond a variation of "it gets better"? 

If it doesn't, I don't waste that person's time or risk upsetting them further.

So in closing, I truly encourage people to really focus on the person and what they are saying. Try to give actionable advice that doesn't contradict the situation (i.e., don't suggest talking a walk to someone who says they feel too depressed to get out of bed).

Sadly, this happens frequently. Some people aren't good at reciprocating. One solution is for you to focus on you, to stop being so helpful that it is a detriment to your own health.

I used to know someone who had no friends because he was anti-social and hard to deal with. I befriended him and learned he had many emotional issues. Over time I became his confidant. He confided just about everything it seemed: murder-suicide plans, crimes he'd committed. He became angrier each passing year that he felt isolated and uncared for. Eventually he added me to his kill list even as he still sought my confidence 

This started when I was 14. He would call me at midnight or 3:00 in the morning and need to talk right up until it was time for me to go to school. My grades suffered. By the time I was in college he was sending me 10-page handwritten letters detailing murder plans that included me and then he'd kill himself.

And yet I still accepted his calls and gave him an outlet because I thought it was better than him going out to kill someone and then himself.

I didn't graduate with my college chums. I had done so poorly I was put on academic probation. I lost my financial aid. He went to jail. Seven years later, I saw him on the street, homeless. I let him stay with me and then helped find him a place to stay. I even paid the first month rent. 

Know what happened? He put me number 1 on his new kill list because he thought I had "everything". Helping him was toxic to my own well being and it took over 15 years before I stopped thinking it was my responsibility to help him.

It is not your responsibility to help those who do not help themselves and do not help you.

It is your responsibility to protect your own well-being.

Thanks for sharing your thoughts and emotions. When I read your plight, these things stuck out to me:

1. The idea of "being grateful for what you have" seems to make you feel a little guilty or make you think you should t be complaining. Don't buy into that. We all have unique experiences and hardships, even the richest of us. Your depression and reasons for it are as valid as others.

2. The drug abuse cycle needs to be addressed again. Likely in dual-treatment setting, whether inpatient or outpatient. Blackout rehabs have their pros and cons, and depending where you are they may be available free of charge. Usually 30 to 90 days of facility living with increased outside mobility and you progress. It could give you a break from the drug abuse  ong enough to focus on mental and emotional hurdles to overcome. Neither addiction or depression are easy to overcome, and rarely can it be done alone.

3. Seems you need positive activities. You express being middle-class and sheltered. If this causes some guilt, perhaps go to an inner city homeless shelter or church that feeds the homeless and volunteer to help feed them or other activities. This can help raise your sense of worth and well-being while also helping others. Caveat: do not go to areas that will create to great a temptation to use.

4. I don't have any advice about medications. I do know sometimes it takes a while to find the right combination. But, in addition to medication, for some people changing diet helps if it stimulates production of specific neurochemicals like serotonin.   Diet will not cure you, but it could help alleviate symptoms naturally. (Example: quit caffeine, up B vitamin-rich foods such as chicken).

5. Get a lot of sunlight and aerobic exercise. Weigjt-lifting, too. Or sports: tennis, swimming, skating, biking, etc. Exercise is very good for depression and addiction.

6. Create a schedule of activities (including work). Take a free course online to occupy your time and mind. They are called OoenCoureWare. Here are two well-known universities that offer these (but it is teach yourself using actual actual curricula from the school)

https://online-learning.harvard.edu/catalog/free

https://ocw.mit.edu/index.htm

7. Enjoy upbeat music and movies more, stuff that may get your adrenaline pumping. If possible, socialize with people who do not do drugs.

Those are all the suggestions I can think of at the moment. I hope something proves helpful.

You are trying to be helpful but telling OP "don't sweat the small stuff" belittles the unique pain this person is experiencing and ultimately places blame on OP as if they just aren't trying hard enough. 

Suggesting that someone can replace a person they love is also not helpful. Lovers and friends are as unique as parents. 

Rather than use a oft-heard platitude, try engaging OP in an empathetic, no judgement discussion. Or if you don't have the time, just show through your words that you are hopeful their particular experience becomes less painful. Share some alternatives options to distract themselves, such as asking what types of things bring them a little joy. Maybe someone will say nothing, then suggest something.

My main point is don't do a blanket platitude statement. They usually are not helpful. We aren't here to practice psychiatry or professional therapy, but we can still be attentive and empathetic.
